title: How to Find, Share, and Govern Google Meet Recordings October 2026
summary: Struggling to find or share a Google Meet recording? This October 2026 guide covers access, sharing, compliance, and governance.
body_markdown:
Google Meet recordings don’t disappear, they just end up somewhere most of your team can’t reach. By default, every recording drops into the host’s personal Drive, which means access, sharing, and visibility all depend on one person remembering to do the right thing. If that feels like a shaky foundation for your meeting data, here’s how to find and share recordings, and how Spinach AI, the system of record for conversation data, replaces per-host Drive folders with one governed record.


**TLDR:**


- Google Meet saves recordings to the host’s personal Drive in a “Meet Recordings” folder, not a shared org location
- Recording requires Google Workspace Business Standard or higher, host or co-host role, and admin permissions turned on
- Missing recordings trace to 5 causes: wrong role, full Drive storage, still processing, wrong account, or admin policy
- GDPR treats meeting recordings as personal data, triggering lawful basis, consent, and retention obligations
- Spinach AI is the enterprise system of record for conversation data: deployed company-wide, it joins Google Meet calls, captures during the meeting, and delivers decisions, action items with named owners, and summaries routed to Slack, Jira, or CRM at meeting end


## Where Google Meet Recordings Are Saved


Google Meet saves recordings directly to the host’s Google Drive, inside a folder called “Meet Recordings.” The file lands there automatically once the meeting ends, and a link is emailed to the host and any co-hosts.


As of July 2026, Google updated this behavior: recordings, transcripts, and Gemini-generated notes are now[organized into a unified per-meeting folder](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2026/07/google-meet-now-organizes-your-meeting-notes-transcripts-and-recordings-in-your-Google-Drive.html) inside Google Drive, so everything from a single call lives in one place.


For teams, the underlying problem remains: the recording lives in the host’s personal Drive. If that person leaves or forgets to share the file, the rest of the team loses access. There’s no org-level location, no centralized library, and no automatic sharing policy. That gap is worth weighing in any[meeting data governance](https://www.spinach.ai/blog/enterprise-meeting-software-buyers-guide) evaluation.


## Who Can Record in Google Meet


Three things gate native Google Meet recording, and if any one of them is wrong, the record button stays greyed out.


- Plan: Recording requires Google Workspace Business Standard or higher. Business Starter and free Gmail accounts do not include it.
- Role: Only the host or a co-host can start a recording. Being a participant on an eligible plan is not enough.
- Admin settings: A Google Workspace admin can disable recording for the entire organization, overriding plan and role entirely.


If your record button is greyed out, check these three in order. Plan tier is the most common culprit, followed by admin policy.


## How to Access and Find Google Meet Recordings


There are three ways to find a recording after a Google Meet ends.


- Google Drive: Go to “My Drive” and open the “Meet Recordings” folder. The file will be labeled with the meeting name and date.
- Calendar event: Open the original Google Calendar event. A link to the recording is added automatically after the meeting ends.
- Email notification: The host receives an email from Google with a direct link to the recording in Drive. Co-hosts get this too.


Processing time varies by file size. Short meetings usually appear within minutes; longer ones can take a few hours. Only the host and co-hosts receive the Drive link by default, so other participants need the host to share it manually.


## How to Share and Download Google Meet Recordings


Once the recording lands in Drive, sharing it works like any other Drive file.


Open the file in the “Meet Recordings” folder, click Share, and choose one of three options:


- Specific people: Enter email contacts to grant access individually.
- Link sharing: Generate a link set to “Viewer,” “Commenter,” or “Editor” access so anyone with the link can open it.
- Domain-wide: Restrict or open access to everyone in your Google Workspace org.


To download, open the file in Drive, click the three-dot menu, and select Download. The file saves locally as an MP4.


The real ceiling here is the host’s attention. Every share is a manual action. If the host forgets, is out of office, or leaves the company, the recording sits inaccessible in their Drive with no org-level rule to automatically share it with attendees or route it to a team channel.


## How to Turn On Recording in Google Meet as an Admin


Admins control recording permissions from the Google Admin console, not from Meet itself. The path is: Admin console > Apps > Google Workspace > Google Meet > Meet video settings > Recording.


From there you have two options: turn on recording for the entire org, or restrict it to specific organizational units. The second option matters for companies that want to allow recording in sales or executive meetings but lock it down elsewhere.


A few things worth knowing before you toggle anything:


- Changes typically propagate quickly across the org, but active meetings are not affected until the next session.
- Only users on eligible Workspace tiers (Business Standard and above) will see the record button even after you turn it on.
- Recording can be activated at the OU level, so different policies can apply to different departments without affecting the entire domain.


One setting that changed in March 2026: Google[changed Meet recording download defaults](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2026/03/upcoming-change-to-default-setting-for-downloading-Google-Meet-recordings.html) , restricting downloads by default for organizations that had not explicitly configured this setting. Admins who want to allow external downloads need to verify that permission is still active in the Admin console under Drive and Docs sharing settings.


## Why Google Meet Recordings Go Missing or Don’t Show Up


A recording that vanishes after a Google Meet usually traces back to one of these causes:

Check the host’s Drive storage first, then look under “Meet Recordings” in the account that was active during the call. If the folder is empty and storage is fine, wait a few hours before assuming the file is lost.


## The Organizational Problem Native Recordings Create


At a company running dozens of meetings per week, the “Meet Recordings” folder pattern breaks fast. Every recording lands in a different host’s Drive. No central inventory exists. No automatic sharing policy routes files to attendees. Whether a new hire can access context from a meeting held three weeks before they joined depends entirely on whether the original host thought to share the file.


When someone leaves the company, their Drive goes with them, and so do the recordings they hosted. There’s no handoff, no transfer, no way for an admin to query what got recorded last quarter without chasing individual accounts.


Searching across recordings isn’t possible in native Meet. You can search Drive file names, but the content inside each video is invisible to search. If you want to know what was decided across six product reviews in Q2, someone has to watch six videos.


The recording exists, but the organization doesn’t own it in any practical sense. That’s a data architecture problem, not a workflow inconvenience, and it’s why organizations end up building a[meeting system of record](https://www.spinach.ai/blog/meeting-system-of-record-enterprise) instead of relying on scattered Drive folders.


## Recording Consent and Compliance Requirements


Recording a meeting is legal in most jurisdictions. Doing it at scale, without a governance layer, is where organizations run into trouble.


Under GDPR, a meeting recording that captures names, voices, or identifiable content is personal data from the moment it starts. That triggers three obligations: a lawful basis for processing ([Article 6](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-6-gdpr/) ), transparent notification to every participant (Article 13), and a defined retention period after which the file must be deleted (Article 5(1)(e)). Keeping recordings in a personal Drive folder indefinitely satisfies none of these, which explains why legal and procurement teams treat recording policy as a blocker.


US-based organizations face a parallel layer. Multiparty-consent states, including[California](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN%C2%A7ionNum=632.) and[Illinois](https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/ilcs/ilcs3.asp?ActID=1006&ChapterID=22) , require affirmative notification to all participants before recording begins. A bot that silently joins without surfacing a clear in-meeting indicator can expose the organization to liability regardless of what the Workspace admin had configured.


These are organizational compliance obligations, not individual decisions left to whoever clicks record. If 200 people are hosting recorded meetings per week under different assumptions about consent and retention, the organization doesn’t have a[meeting recording consent policy](https://www.spinach.ai/blog/meeting-recording-consent-it-policy) . It has 200 individual habits.


## Retention, Access Control, and Governance at Scale


Google Drive does not automatically delete old recordings, restrict access by sensitivity tier, or log who opened a file. Those controls exist in the Google Workspace ecosystem, but they require deliberate configuration.


Google Workspace Vault covers Meet recordings in three ways, and the third is a gap:


- eDiscovery and litigation holds: Vault handles both, but only if an admin set retention rules before the recording was created.
- Preservation: Vault can preserve files against deletion and support legal holds.
- Classification and access: Vault does not classify recordings by sensitivity or restrict access based on meeting type. That work falls on the admin.


Drive retention policies can enforce deletion schedules, but they apply broadly. A single rule set across the “Meet Recordings” folder hits sales calls and HR conversations the same way. Compliance-heavy environments typically need tiered retention: shorter windows for routine standups, longer holds for board-level or compliance-relevant discussions. That is the kind of[data retention for enterprise AI tools](https://www.spinach.ai/blog/enterprise-data-retention-policy) that native Workspace settings don’t configure on their own. Native Google Workspace does not configure that distinction without substantial admin effort and Vault licensing.


Access control defaults to the host’s judgment. There is no org-level rule that says “recordings containing external participants require explicit approval before sharing” or “HR meeting recordings are restricted to the People team.” Those guardrails have to be built manually and rebuilt every time an admin turns over, which is why[governing meeting data at scale](https://www.spinach.ai/blog/governing-meeting-data-at-scale) requires more than default Drive settings.


For IT and legal teams working through[meeting recording security and compliance](https://www.spinach.ai/blog/enterprise-meeting-recording-security-compliance-guide) requirements, the building blocks are there in native Meet infrastructure, but they require active governance architecture to function. Out of the box, what you have is a folder of MP4 files with no classification, no automatic access tiering, no audit log, and no enforced deletion schedule.


## Turning Raw Recordings Into Structured, Searchable Meeting Data


A recording file is the starting point, not the destination. An MP4 sitting in Drive requires someone to rewatch it, scrub through timestamps, and manually pull out what matters. At scale, that process doesn’t happen, and the organizational value of the meeting disappears with it.


The gap between “recording exists” and “organization learned something” is where most teams lose ground. Transcription closes part of it, since a text file is searchable in ways a video is not. But a transcript alone still requires someone to read through it, interpret what was decided, and route that information to the right people and tools by hand.


What actually moves the needle is converting the raw recording into outputs the organization can act on without a human relay step: decisions tagged with owners, action items pushed to Jira or Linear with the right assignee and context, a summary delivered to Slack before the team moves on to the next call, CRM records updated with what a customer said without a rep re-entering it from memory two hours later.


That is the difference between a recording as an archive and a recording as a data source: the core premise behind[enterprise conversation intelligence](https://www.spinach.ai/blog/conversation-intelligence-enterprise-guide) . The former requires someone to go looking for information. The latter routes information to whoever needs it, in the system they already use, without waiting for a follow-up that may or may not arrive. That distinction is worth understanding before selecting any[conversation intelligence](https://www.spinach.ai/blog/enterprise-conversation-intelligence-buyers-guide) platform.

## Final Thoughts on Google Meet Recording Access and Governance


The record button in Google Meet is just the beginning. Where the file goes, who can access it, how long it stays there, and whether anyone can search what was said inside it are all separate questions, and native Meet leaves most of them unanswered by default. For small teams, that’s manageable. For organizations with compliance requirements or more than a handful of recorded meetings per week, it’s a gap worth closing deliberately. **Why is my Google Meet recording not showing up in Drive after the meeting ended?**


The most common reasons a Google Meet recording doesn’t appear in Google Drive are: the recorder was a participant instead of the host or co-host, the host’s Drive storage was full at the time of the call, or the file is still processing. Longer recordings can take several hours to appear in the “Meet Recordings” folder, so wait before assuming the file is lost. Check which Google account was active during the meeting. If the host is signed into multiple accounts, the recording may have saved to a Drive they’re not currently viewing.


**Where do Google Meet recordings go, and how do you find them?**


Google Meet recordings save automatically to the host’s Google Drive inside a folder called “Meet Recordings,” labeled with the meeting name and date. You can also find the recording link in the original Google Calendar event or in the email Google sends to the host and co-hosts at meeting end. Note that only the host and co-hosts receive that link by default. Other attendees need the host to share it manually, which means access depends entirely on one person remembering to act.


**How do I record a Google Meet if I’m not the host, or if my record button is greyed out?**


Native Google Meet recording requires three conditions to be met simultaneously: a Google Workspace Business Standard plan or higher, host or co-host status in the meeting, and recording turned on by the Workspace admin. If any one of those is missing, the record button stays greyed out. If you’re a participant without host permissions, you cannot start a native recording. Your options are to ask the host to record, request co-host status before the call starts, or use a Google Meet recording extension that captures at the browser or system level instead of relying on Meet’s built-in controls.

The gap is architectural: one approach produces a folder of MP4 files; the other produces governed, queryable conversation data the organization owns and can act on.


**How do I turn on recording in Google Meet for my organization, and what changed in 2026?**


Recording is controlled from the Google Admin console under Apps > Google Workspace > Google Meet > Meet video settings > Recording, not from Meet itself. You can turn it on for the entire org or restrict it to specific organizational units, which matters if you want to allow recording in sales or executive meetings while locking it down elsewhere. One change to know about: Google updated default download behavior for Meet recordings in March 2026, restricting external downloads by default for organizations that had not explicitly configured that setting. If your users report that downloads are blocked, verify the permission is still active in the Admin console under Drive and Docs sharing settings.


**Do Google Meet recordings save automatically, or does someone have to start them manually?**


Recording never starts automatically. A host or co-host on an eligible Workspace plan has to click record for every call, and the file only saves to Drive after that person stops it or the meeting ends.


**How long does it take for a Google Meet recording to show up in Drive?**


Short calls usually appear in the “Meet Recordings” folder within minutes, while longer meetings can take a few hours to finish processing. If it has been several hours and the file still isn’t there, check Drive storage on the host account before assuming something went wrong.


**How do I record a Google Meet on my phone with audio?**


Native Meet recording works the same on the mobile app as it does on desktop, provided you’re the host or co-host on Business Standard or higher and admin permissions allow it, and it captures audio by default. On iPhone and Android, the control sits in the same three-dot menu inside the call.


**Is there a free way to record Google Meet calls?**


Native Google Meet recording requires a paid Business Standard plan or higher, so it isn’t free on a personal or free Gmail account. A browser-based Google Meet recording extension is the usual workaround for anyone without an eligible Workspace tier.


**How do I record a Google Meet on my laptop without a Workspace premium plan?**


Without Business Standard or higher, the built-in record button won’t appear, so you need a separate capture method: a browser extension, your operating system’s screen recorder (QuickTime on Mac, Xbox Game Bar on Windows 11), or third-party recording software running alongside the call.


**Are Google Meet recording Chrome extensions safe to use?**


Safety depends entirely on the extension’s permissions and publisher, since recorder extensions typically require access to your screen, microphone, and sometimes your Google account. Check reviews, confirm the developer is verified, and avoid extensions asking for Drive-wide access they don’t need before installing one for free recording.


**Why would I use a recording extension instead of Google Meet’s built-in recorder?**


A Google Meet recording extension lets you capture a call even when you’re not the host, when your Workspace plan doesn’t include recording, or when an admin has disabled it organization-wide. The tradeoff is that extension-captured files save locally or to the extension’s own storage, not automatically into the shared “Meet Recordings” folder structure.


**Should I rely on Google Drive’s built-in sharing or build a central recordings library instead?**


Drive’s built-in sharing works fine for a single meeting shared with a handful of people, but it breaks down once dozens of hosts are each individually responsible for sharing their own files. Teams running more than a few recorded meetings a week typically need a governed, centralized record instead of relying on every host to remember to click share.


**Do Google Meet recordings count against my Google Drive storage limit?**


Yes, every recording saved to the “Meet Recordings” folder counts against the host’s Drive storage quota, not a separate organizational pool. That’s also why a full Drive is one of the most common reasons a recording silently fails to save.


**Can I record a Google Meet on an iPad with audio?**


Yes, if you’re the host or co-host with an eligible plan, the Meet app on iPad supports the same native record function as iPhone and desktop, capturing audio and video together. If you’re a participant without host rights, you’ll need the host to record or use a separate screen-recording app on the device.
